source: The Cosmic Distance Ladder
Parallax calibrates Cepheids, Cepheids calibrate type Ia supernovae, and each rung reaches farther.
Students think one method measures distances all the way out.

No single method measures every cosmic distance. Astronomers build a distance ladder: each rung uses a method that works over some range, calibrated by the rung below it where their ranges overlap. You met the standard candles; the distance modulus turns each one into a distance.

A standard candle is an object whose absolute magnitude $M$ we know; measure its apparent magnitude $m$ and $d = 10^{(m - M + 5)/5}$ pc. But to know $M$, you must first measure the distance to some examples by another method. Parallax, pure geometry, gives distances to nearby Cepheid variable stars (Gaia measures parallaxes for over a billion stars). Those Cepheids calibrate Henrietta Leavitt's period–luminosity relation (1912), so Cepheids in galaxies tens of megaparsecs away give those galaxies' distances. Type Ia supernovae that explode in those same galaxies calibrate the supernovae's peak brightness, about $M = -19.3$, and supernovae can be seen billions of light-years away.

Parallax → Cepheids → type Ia supernovae → Hubble's law. Each rung is only as good as the one beneath it: an error in a lower rung carries up into every distance above it, including the Hubble constant.
The rungs of the distance ladder and the ranges where each works. Overlaps between rungs are where one calibrates the next.
A Cepheid's brightness rises and falls with a regular period. The longer the period, the more luminous the star.
Worked examples
A Cepheid pulsates every 30 days and has average apparent magnitude 25.0. Use $M_V = -2.43(\log_{10}P - 1) - 4.05$.
A Cepheid in a distant galaxy
About 11 Mpc, roughly 36 million light-years.
A type Ia supernova peaks at $m = 19.0$. With $M = -19.3$, how far away is it?
A supernova much farther out
About 460 Mpc, roughly 1.5 billion light-years, far beyond the reach of Cepheids.
If the Cepheid calibration is off by 0.10 magnitude, how much are all the distances above it off?
How errors climb the ladder
About 5% for every distance above, and 5% in the Hubble constant. That is why so much work goes into the lowest rungs.
A magnitude error $\Delta$ is a distance factor $10^{\Delta/5} = 10^{0.02}$.

Thinking one method measures distances all the way out. Parallax angles become too small to measure beyond a few thousand parsecs; individual Cepheids become too faint beyond about 40 Mpc; supernovae are rare and must be calibrated by Cepheids first. Every far distance therefore rests on all the rungs beneath it. Check any quoted distance by asking which method measured it, and what calibrated that method.
